\setstretch{1}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-technology-futures
#| tbl-cap: "Technologies, educational settings, and future horizons by outlet group, n (%)."

result_table(c("Technological object", "Educational context", "Timespan", "Space"))
```

\endgroup

*Note.* Cells report n (%); denominators are `r nrow(main)` overall, `r sum(main$outlet_group == "public/central")` public/central, and `r sum(main$outlet_group == "commercial/general")` commercial/general. Multiple codes can occur in one article. “AI form unspecified” records a source referring to AI without identifying its technical form; missing coding is reported separately. “AI form unspecified” can coexist with a specified form when different statements in the same article discuss AI at different levels of specificity.

The source accounts showed how the scope of a proposal shaped its technological detail. The Dân trí student account concerned the named tool ChatGPT and its use in study ([DTR24_022](https://dantri.com.vn/giao-duc/dung-chatgpt-lam-bai-sinh-vien-hoang-khi-kien-thuc-vao-nhanh-di-voi-20241113100850798.htm)). Reporting on an AI competency framework instead discussed the knowledge, ethics, and skills pupils would need across applications. The director of the Vietnam National Institute of Educational Sciences described adapting UNESCO’s framework to Vietnamese education, and the article connected this work to curriculum design, teacher preparation, and computing infrastructure ([GDT24_000](https://giaoducthoidai.vn/khung-nang-luc-tri-tue-nhan-tao-cho-hoc-sinh-hieu-va-lam-chu-cong-nghe-post705947.html)). The future concerned a programme of educational preparation extending beyond any single product.

Temporal accounts ranged from present implementation to dated policy goals. Futures being implemented or realised appeared in `r pct("timespan__TIME_IMMEDIATE")`% of articles. Explicit dates, intervals, or stages without a stated classification of proximity appeared in `r pct("timespan__TIME_ANCHORED_UNCLASSIFIED")`%; explicitly near-term and distant futures appeared in `r pct("timespan__TIME_NEAR")`% and `r pct("timespan__TIME_DISTANT")`%, respectively. Timespan was unassigned in `r pct("timespan__missing")`%. Public/central articles more frequently described implementation and explicitly long-term futures, while commercial/general articles more frequently left timespan unassigned.

Reporting on the education ministry’s draft AI strategy supplied a dated system-wide ambition:

> Looking towards 2035, AI will become a common tool for every learner, teacher, and education manager, while an AI ecosystem developed by Vietnamese enterprises will be used consistently across general education.
>
> — Report on the education ministry’s draft AI strategy, *Giáo dục Việt Nam* ([GDN25_005](https://giaoduc.net.vn/bo-giao-duc-va-dao-tao-xay-dung-chien-luoc-ung-dung-ai-trong-giao-duc-post250172.gd))

The same article set out policy development, training, infrastructure, and partnerships as routes towards that goal. A Kênh 14 report on Japan supplied a different scale and horizon: a planned trial of AI-enabled English-teaching robots in approximately 500 schools from April 2019 ([KEN18_001](https://kenh14.vn/di-truoc-nen-giao-duc-cua-the-gioi-nhat-ban-se-dung-robot-co-tri-tue-nhan-tao-de-day-tieng-anh-cho-hoc-sinh-o-500-truong-hoc-2018082709585758.chn)). It attributed the proposal to constraints on recruiting native-speaking teachers and connected deployment to access and language learning. The two reports made the future concrete through different objects: a national educational ecosystem and a scheduled school-level trial.

Vietnam was the stated geographical reach in `r pct("space__SPACE_VIETNAM")`% of articles, specific foreign countries in `r pct("space__SPACE_FOREIGN_DOMESTIC")`%, and cross-national or global settings in `r pct("space__SPACE_TRANSNATIONAL")`%. Public/central coverage more frequently situated futures in Vietnam (`r pct("space__SPACE_VIETNAM", filter(main, outlet_group == "public/central"))`%, compared with `r pct("space__SPACE_VIETNAM", filter(main, outlet_group == "commercial/general"))`%). Commercial/general coverage more frequently situated them in named foreign countries. Vietnamese news therefore brought domestic plans and overseas educational proposals into the same field of coverage.

## Voices, proposed actions, and responsibilities

Learners were identified as affected by educational AI futures in `r pct("affected_entities__AFFECT_LEARNER")`% of articles, appeared as speakers in `r pct("speaker__SPK_LEARNER")`%, and were assigned responsibility in `r pct("responsibility__RESP_LEARNER")`%. Coverage discussed their anticipated experiences much more frequently than it included their expectations. Their assigned responsibilities also appeared more frequently than their own speaking positions.

Educators, researchers, and specialists articulated futures in `r pct("speaker__SPK_ACADEMIC_EXPERT")`% of articles, educational institutions or leaders in `r pct("speaker__SPK_ED_LEADERSHIP")`%, and public authorities in `r pct("speaker__SPK_PUBLIC")`%. Commercial actors appeared in `r pct("speaker__SPK_BUSINESS")`% and families or caregivers in `r pct("speaker__SPK_FAMILY")`%. The article’s narrative or editorial voice advanced future claims in `r pct("speaker__SPK_AUTHOR")`% (@tbl-actors-implications).

\clearpage

\begingroup
\setstretch{1}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-actors-implications
#| tbl-cap: "Voices, proposed actions, and responsibilities by outlet group, n (%)."

result_table(c("Speaker", "Action", "Responsibility"))
```

\endgroup

*Note.* Cells report n (%); denominators are `r nrow(main)` overall, `r sum(main$outlet_group == "public/central")` public/central, and `r sum(main$outlet_group == "commercial/general")` commercial/general. Frequencies count the presence of speaking positions and assigned responsibilities, not individual speakers or shares of quoted text. Multiple codes are permitted.

Public/central coverage more frequently included public authorities and educational leadership. Commercial/general coverage more frequently included experts and learners. Learner voices appeared in `r pct("speaker__SPK_LEARNER", filter(main, outlet_group == "commercial/general"))`% of commercial/general articles and `r pct("speaker__SPK_LEARNER", filter(main, outlet_group == "public/central"))`% of public/central articles. The Dân trí account above illustrates what a learner’s contribution added: a concern grounded in using ChatGPT and subsequently forgetting the material. In reporting on institutional programmes, by contrast, leaders described the competencies learners should acquire and the opportunities those competencies would provide.

Educational organisations were most frequently assigned responsibility (`r pct("responsibility__RESP_ED_ORG")`%), followed by educational workers (`r pct("responsibility__RESP_ED_WORKER")`%), learners (`r pct("responsibility__RESP_LEARNER")`%), public authorities (`r pct("responsibility__RESP_PUBLIC")`%), and commercial actors (`r pct("responsibility__RESP_BUSINESS")`%). Public/central coverage more often assigned action to public authorities and educational organisations; commercial/general coverage more often assigned it to learners. Reporting on the ministry’s draft strategy explicitly placed teachers and education managers in the lead:

> Teachers and education managers play a pioneering role in applying AI to professional work and guiding learners to use AI responsibly. In particular, for school pupils, AI use must be closely controlled to avoid negative effects.
>
> — Report on the education ministry’s draft AI strategy, *Giáo dục Việt Nam* ([GDN25_005](https://giaoduc.net.vn/bo-giao-duc-va-dao-tao-xay-dung-chien-luoc-ung-dung-ai-trong-giao-duc-post250172.gd))

The article also called for teachers to update their teaching and assessment practices, for institutions to establish rules, and for businesses to develop educational systems. Its proposal distributed different tasks across actors while placing supervision of learners within education.

Recommendations focused more often on changing teaching, learning, or assessment (`r pct("action__ACT_PRACTICE")`%) and providing resources (`r pct("action__ACT_RESOURCES")`%) than on evaluating AI interventions (`r pct("action__ACT_EVALUATE")`%). Rules and safeguards also appeared more frequently (`r pct("action__ACT_RULES")`%) than intervention evaluation. This contrast concerns reported recommendations, not whether evaluation occurred in practice. Public/central coverage contained all six action categories more frequently, with larger differences for curriculum, resources, and coordination than for educational practice.

Assessment proposals gave these actions distinct forms. Báo Chính phủ described police coordination with the education sector, detection equipment, and guidance for examination staff to prevent technology-enabled cheating ([BCP26_009](https://baochinhphu.vn/bo-cong-an-siet-chat-chong-gian-lan-bang-ai-tai-ky-thi-tot-nghiep-thpt-102260610082735862.htm)). A Tia Sáng account instead questioned the grounds on which teachers judged suspected AI-generated writing:

> Once teachers stop asking “what were you thinking when you wrote this passage?” and look only at the percentage displayed on the screen, the relationship between teacher and learner will cease to be education and become control.
>
> — Authorial commentary, *Tia Sáng* ([TSG25_001](https://tiasang.com.vn/sinh-vien-viet-hay-bi-nghi-dung-ai-ai-co-quyen-phan-xet-4966355.html))

One report described detection equipment and police coordination for examination security. The other argued that teachers should ask students to explain their work rather than rely on a detector’s percentage. The latter is an illustrative critical commentary within the public/central group, not evidence of how common that position was across its outlets.

Speaking capacity did not exhaust institutional affiliation. The VnExpress account of teachers’ professional work came from a VioEdu/FPT representative, and the competition account in Giáo dục Việt Nam came from an FPT University leader. Educational expertise and organisational interests appeared together in these sources. Source comparisons also identified repeated learner accounts in CFE26_012 and KEN26_015, shared competition-launch material in GDN25_006, KEN25_010, and VNN25_004, and overlapping official implementation guidance in GDT26_024, GDT26_025, and LDG26_009. These examples show how particular voices and proposals circulated across publications as well as how they were distributed between outlet groups.

## Recurrent code combinations and their prominence

```{r}
#| label: setup-configurations
#| include: false
statement_records <- purrr::map_dfr(coded_records, function(record) {
  purrr::map_dfr(seq_along(record$accounts), function(i) {
    unit <- record$accounts[[i]]
    tibble(article_id = record$ID, statement = i, position = unit$position,
           codes = list(unit$codes))
  })
})
configuration_specs <- list(
  development = c(future_role = "FR_HUMAN_DEVELOPMENT", desirability = "DES_POSITIVE",
    rationale = "RATION_PEDAGOGY", action = "ACT_PRACTICE"),
  work = c(future_role = "FR_WORK_LIVELIHOODS", desirability = "DES_POSITIVE",
    rationale = "RATION_ECONOMY", action = "ACT_CURRICULUM"),
  judgment = c(future_role = "FR_TRUSTWORTHY_JUDGMENT", desirability = "DES_POSITIVE",
    rationale = "RATION_RIGHTS_INTEGRITY", action = "ACT_RULES"),
  developmental_warning = c(future_role = "FR_HUMAN_DEVELOPMENT", desirability = "DES_NEGATIVE",
    rationale = "RATION_PEDAGOGY"),
  judgment_warning = c(future_role = "FR_TRUSTWORTHY_JUDGMENT", desirability = "DES_NEGATIVE",
    rationale = "RATION_RIGHTS_INTEGRITY")
)
configuration_labels <- c(
  development = "Human development; positive; learning quality; changed practice",
  work = "Work preparation; positive; economic returns; curriculum change",
  judgment = "Trustworthy judgment; positive; rights and integrity; rules",
  developmental_warning = "Human development; negative; learning quality",
  judgment_warning = "Trustworthy judgment; negative; rights and integrity")
configuration_matches <- purrr::imap(configuration_specs, function(spec, key) {
  statement_records |> filter(purrr::map_lgl(codes, function(codes)
    all(vapply(names(spec), function(field) spec[[field]] %in% unlist(codes[[field]]), logical(1)))))
})
configuration_counts <- purrr::imap_dfr(configuration_matches, function(rows, key) {
  tibble(key, configuration = configuration_labels[[key]],
    articles = n_distinct(rows$article_id),
    primary = n_distinct(rows$article_id[rows$position == "primary"]))
})
config_n <- function(key, column = "articles")
  configuration_counts[[column]][match(key, configuration_counts$key)]
config_actor <- function(key, field, code) {
  rows <- configuration_matches[[key]]
  n_distinct(rows$article_id[purrr::map_lgl(rows$codes,
    function(x) code %in% unlist(x[[field]]))])
}
# Enumerate all four-field combinations before identifying the leading one.
four_field_counts <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(statement_records)), function(i) {
  codes <- statement_records$codes[[i]]
  values <- lapply(c("future_role", "desirability", "rationale", "action"),
    function(field) setdiff(unlist(codes[[field]]), "MISSING"))
  names(values) <- c("role", "evaluation", "rationale", "action")
  if (any(lengths(values) == 0)) return(tibble())
  as_tibble(do.call(expand.grid, c(values, stringsAsFactors = FALSE))) |>
    mutate(article_id = statement_records$article_id[[i]])
}) |> distinct() |> count(role, evaluation, rationale, action, sort = TRUE)
stopifnot(four_field_counts$n[[1]] == config_n("development"),
          four_field_counts$role[[1]] == "FR_HUMAN_DEVELOPMENT",
          all(configuration_counts$primary <= configuration_counts$articles))
positive_primary <- sum(purrr::map_lgl(statement_records$codes,
  function(x) "DES_POSITIVE" %in% unlist(x$desirability)) & statement_records$position == "primary")
negative_primary <- sum(purrr::map_lgl(statement_records$codes,
  function(x) "DES_NEGATIVE" %in% unlist(x$desirability)) & statement_records$position == "primary")
```

The most frequent four-field combination linked human development, a positive evaluation, learning quality, and changes to teaching, learning, or assessment. It appeared within the same statement in `r config_n("development")` articles (`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * config_n("development") / nrow(main))`% of the corpus) and occupied the primary position in `r config_n("development", "primary")` articles (@tbl-configurations). This connection joins a valued educational outcome to both a reason for pursuing it and a proposed change in practice.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-configurations
#| tbl-cap: "Selected code combinations within the same statement and their primary-position counts. Each cell counts articles, once per combination."
configuration_counts |>
  transmute(Configuration = configuration,
    All = sprintf("%d (%.1f)", articles, 100 * articles / nrow(main)),
    Primary = sprintf("%d (%.1f)", primary, 100 * primary / nrow(main))) |>
  kbl(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE, linesep = "",
    col.names = c("Linked fields", "Any statement, n (%)", "Primary, n (%)")) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "repeat_header", font_size = 9) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "8cm")
```

*Note.* Percentages use all `r nrow(main)` articles. Primary counts are subsets of the corresponding any-statement counts. Code combinations overlap. The first three rows specify an action; warning rows leave action unrestricted so that warnings without recommendations remain visible. The rows are selected pathways and contrasts, not an exhaustive ranking or mutually exclusive types.

The leading combination distributed educational work across several actors. Within its matching statements, educators, researchers, or specialists spoke in `r config_actor("development", "speaker", "SPK_ACADEMIC_EXPERT")` articles and educational leaders in `r config_actor("development", "speaker", "SPK_ED_LEADERSHIP")`. Responsibility was assigned to educational workers in `r config_actor("development", "responsibility", "RESP_ED_WORKER")`, learners in `r config_actor("development", "responsibility", "RESP_LEARNER")`, and educational organisations in `r config_actor("development", "responsibility", "RESP_ED_ORG")`. These roles belong to the same statements as the developmental promise, rather than being inferred from separate passages in the article.

Two further combinations specified routes through curricula and governance. Work preparation, positive evaluation, economic returns, and curriculum change co-occurred in `r config_n("work")` articles, including `r config_n("work", "primary")` primary statements. Educational organisations were assigned responsibility within these statements in `r config_actor("work", "responsibility", "RESP_ED_ORG")` articles. Trustworthy judgment, positive evaluation, rights and integrity, and rules co-occurred in `r config_n("judgment")` articles, including `r config_n("judgment", "primary")` primary statements. Public authorities spoke within this combination in `r config_actor("judgment", "speaker", "SPK_PUBLIC")` articles, while educational organisations were assigned responsibility in `r config_actor("judgment", "responsibility", "RESP_ED_ORG")`.

Warnings formed recurrent connections of their own. Human development, negative evaluation, and learning quality co-occurred in `r config_n("developmental_warning")` articles, with `r config_n("developmental_warning", "primary")` in the primary position. Trustworthy judgment, negative evaluation, and rights and integrity co-occurred in `r config_n("judgment_warning")`, with `r config_n("judgment_warning", "primary")` primary. Across all primary statements, positive evaluations appeared in `r positive_primary` articles (`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * positive_primary / nrow(main))`%) and negative evaluations in `r negative_primary` (`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * negative_primary / nrow(main))`%). Among the `r sum(main$desirability__DES_NEGATIVE == 1, na.rm = TRUE)` articles containing negative evaluations, `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * negative_primary / sum(main$desirability__DES_NEGATIVE == 1, na.rm = TRUE))`% placed a negative evaluation in the primary position. The corresponding proportion for articles containing positive evaluations was `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * positive_primary / sum(main$desirability__DES_POSITIVE == 1, na.rm = TRUE))`%. Positive evaluations thus appeared in the primary position in most articles containing them; negative evaluations usually appeared only in secondary statements.

Alternative arrangements also carried positive evaluations. Both the examination-security report (BCP26_009) and the Tia Sáng commentary (TSG25_001) matched the trustworthy-judgment combination with rules. The former proposed detection and coordination to protect examinations; the latter proposed restrictions on detector-based judgment alongside dialogue and process-based assessment. Similarly, the legal-education report (GDN25_023) placed responsible AI use and human judgment in its primary arrangement, while warnings about junior lawyers’ dependence appeared in secondary statements. The same broad codes thus accommodated different arrangements, and criticism could accompany a positive proposal within one article.

## Sensitivity of the outlet comparison

```{r}
#| label: setup-sensitivity
#| include: false
primary <- main
for (record in coded_records) {
  selected <- Filter(function(unit) identical(unit$position, "primary"), record$accounts)
  stopifnot(length(selected) == 1L)
  i <- match(record$ID, primary$article_id)
  for (field in names(selected[[1]]$codes)) {
    values <- setdiff(unlist(selected[[1]]$codes[[field]]), "MISSING")
    cols <- grep(paste0("^", field, "__"), names(primary), value = TRUE)
    for (column in cols) {
      suffix <- sub(paste0("^", field, "__"), "", column)
      primary[[column]][i] <- if (suffix == "missing") as.integer(length(values) == 0L) else
        if (length(values)) as.integer(suffix %in% values) else NA_integer_
    }
  }
}
selected_codes <- c("future_role__FR_COLLECTIVE_ADVANCEMENT",
  "technology_object__OBJ_GENERATIVE", "desirability__DES_NEGATIVE",
  "action__ACT_RULES", "action__ACT_EVALUATE")
gap <- function(data, code) {
  a <- data[data$outlet_group == "public/central", ]
  b <- data[data$outlet_group == "commercial/general", ]
  100 * (sum(a[[code]] == 1, na.rm = TRUE) / nrow(a) -
         sum(b[[code]] == 1, na.rm = TRUE) / nrow(b))
}
sensitivity <- purrr::map_dfr(selected_codes, function(code) {
  omitted <- vapply(unique(main$outlet_domain), function(domain)
    gap(main[main$outlet_domain != domain, ], code), numeric(1))
  tibble(code, full = gap(main, code), primary = gap(primary, code),
         low = min(omitted), high = max(omitted))
}) |> left_join(code_labels |> select(code, category), by = "code")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "Selected outlet differences under alternative aggregation and outlet omission (percentage points, public/central minus commercial/general)."
sensitivity |>
  transmute(Category = category, Full = sprintf("%+.1f", full),
    Primary = sprintf("%+.1f", primary),
    Omission = sprintf("%+.1f to %+.1f", low, high)) |>
  kbl(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE, linesep = "",
      col.names = c("Category", "All statements", "Primary only", "Omit one outlet")) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position", font_size = 8) |>
  column_spec(1, width = "5.5cm")
```

All five selected outlet differences retained their direction under primary-only coding and every single-outlet omission (@tbl-sensitivity). Primary-only differences were smaller for collective development, negative evaluations, rules, and intervention evaluation; the generative-AI difference was slightly larger. Negative evaluations appeared in 28.5% of public/central articles and 37.9% of commercial/general articles when all statements were considered, but in only 8.3% and 11.1%, respectively, when counting primary statements. The group difference therefore narrowed from 9.3 to 2.9 percentage points. Negative evaluations were more often present somewhere in an article than attached to its coded primary arrangement in both groups; the additional coverage captured by secondary statements accounted for much of the between-group gap. Primary-only coding narrows the unit to each article’s prominent arrangement; omission ranges show how the full article-level difference changes when one outlet is removed. The ranges are descriptive, not confidence intervals. Neither check removes shared-source articles or changes the main corpus.



# Discussion

A dominant developmental orientation emerges from the coverage: AI is made educationally worthwhile through improvements in human capabilities, supported by changes in practice, curricula, and institutional provision. Its prominence rests on more than the frequency of individual codes. The leading same-statement combination connects human development to a positive evaluation, a pedagogical rationale, and changed educational practice; its speaker and responsibility profiles place educators, learners, and institutions within that project. Positive evaluations also occupy the primary position in 83.0% of articles. Dominance here describes the relative prevalence and prominence of this broad developmental orientation. Its practical forms vary across the proposals that advance it.

This pattern suggests a process of selection among possible educational futures. The future brought to the foreground is one in which educational actors make technological change beneficial by adapting what they do. Questions about learning, skills, and governance are commonly formulated within that direction: which practices should change, which capabilities should be developed, and which institutions should act. In this sense, dominance concerns the terms on which the future is discussed. It gives an implementation-oriented account of educational improvement a privileged position while accommodating disagreement over its form. This connects the study to accounts of how sociotechnical expectations organise present action (Rahm & Rahm-Skågeby, 2023; Hendriks et al., 2025).

Alternative futures remain visible within this dominant orientation. Recurrent warnings connect AI use to losses in human development and trustworthy judgment, while source readings identify proposals to protect independent thinking, restore dialogue, and ground assessment in evidence of learning. These alternatives are not reducible to negative evaluations. A restriction on unreliable detectors can itself be a positively valued future, just as technical controls can be promoted as a route to credible assessment. The contrast lies in the arrangement: whether educational judgment rests on detection and enforcement or on teachers’ engagement with learners’ reasoning. Shared purposes supply a common language through which different futures are advanced.

The distribution of prominence gives these alternatives unequal standing. Negative evaluations appeared in 33.1% of articles but occupied the primary position in 9.7%. Among articles containing negative evaluations, 29.2% placed them in the primary position, compared with 86.4% for positive evaluations among articles containing them. The outlet gap also narrowed from 9.3 to 2.9 percentage points when only primary statements were counted. Criticism circulated more widely than it structured the principal future of an article. The legal-education example makes this relationship concrete: responsible AI use framed the primary arrangement, while dependence and limits on use appeared in secondary positions. The pattern is one of selective foregrounding: an affirmative future holds the centre, while warnings and qualifications often enter around it.

Close reading identifies four practical pathways within this landscape: building educational capacity through resources and curriculum; protecting assessment through technical controls; grounding judgment in dialogue and evidence of learning; and protecting developing capabilities by limiting dependence. These pathways describe practices reconstructed from source passages; the five rows in @tbl-configurations report selected code combinations. They operate at different levels of detail. The combination linking trustworthy judgment, positive evaluation, rights and integrity, and rules includes both technical enforcement and restrictions on detector-based decisions. Close reading distinguishes these pathways within the same broad codes. Efficiency becomes educationally meaningful through the activities it enables or displaces, and assistance becomes problematic when it substitutes for developing judgment (Mamlok, 2025; Wieczorek & Romele, 2026).

The outlet patterns suggest two overlapping reporting registers. A programmatic register connects collective purposes, institutional responsibilities, domestic implementation, and AI described in general terms. An application-and-experience register gives greater prominence to specified tools, overseas examples, and evaluations grounded in use. Public/central and commercial/general coverage give these registers different emphases, but neither register belongs exclusively to one group. This interpretation develops research on national AI aspirations (Bareis & Katzenbach, 2022; Nemorin et al., 2023; Nguyen et al., 2026) without treating institutional labels as ownership categories or assigning each group a single imaginary. National development can support adoption or caution, depending on which practices are thought to build collective capability.

The relative scarcity of explicit intervention evaluation raises a further question about how promised improvement becomes accountable. Rules, resources, and changed practices specify how to act, but do not necessarily specify how educational benefits will be established. The contrast concerns what coverage articulates; it cannot show that institutions failed to evaluate their interventions. In SIPC terms, distinguishing proposed action from evidence of its effects helps identify what remains unspecified when a future is made actionable. Learners’ speaking positions are one part of that question, alongside professional judgment and institutional authority, rather than a separate organising claim for the study.

Temporal variation and source circulation qualify apparent consensus. The prominence of generative AI and negative evaluations in 2023 situates the analysis within a changing mix of educational problems, while later coverage combines those concerns with broader programmes. Repeated event material and official formulations can amplify a proposal without adding independent endorsement. For comparative education, the findings therefore identify ways educational change is publicly justified within one national setting; tracing their subsequent institutional adoption would require evidence beyond news texts.

## Limitations

The corpus is bounded by Google News indexing and per-query retrieval limits, selected domains and vocabulary, title screening, and recoverable article texts. Queries explicitly included assessment and academic-integrity terms, which may have increased the visibility of those concerns; period-specific changes in search vocabulary may also contribute to apparent temporal differences. Attempts to retrieve all available matches do not establish completeness. Sparse early years, the partial 2026 window, and changes in outlet and event composition constrain temporal comparisons. The approximate outlet groups support descriptive comparisons within this corpus, not causal claims about political or commercial influence.

AI-assisted extraction and coding remain interpretive. Independent coding, source-linked evidence, and automated checks supported agreement assessment and traceability. Agreement does not establish validity or eliminate shared omissions. Separate agreement results for primary-position assignment and desirability are not yet documented; the overall coefficient does not establish their field-specific reliability.

Article-level presence gives a brief mention the same weight as an extended argument. Primary position records the coder’s judgment of the prominent arrangement, not a direct measure of headline placement, text length, or editorial intention. Selection and dominance are therefore interpretations of published emphasis; the corpus cannot identify deliberately excluded futures or reconstruct editorial decisions. Linked-statement counts preserve relationships lost in article totals. Their frequency depends on the prevalence and breadth of component codes, and combinations requiring fewer fields are easier to match. The four practical pathways are overlapping source-based interpretations, not categories whose prevalence has been separately coded. Even a shared statement can contain several propositions. Mixed evaluations remain distinct from separate positive and negative statements, and missing fields remain visible in the denominators.

Shared quotations and event material remain in the analytical corpus as instances of circulation. Consequently, repeated coverage is not equivalent to independently originating support; provenance checks on selected cases do not reconstruct all transmission paths. Speaking capacities also need not capture every institutional interest. Finally, public articulation establishes neither audience acceptance nor implementation. Research following proposals into educational practice could examine whether their anticipated benefits and responsibilities materialise.

# Conclusion

A developmental orientation held a prominent place in Vietnamese news coverage. Human development, positive evaluation, pedagogical reasons, and changed practice formed the most frequent four-field combination, while positive futures occupied most primary positions. Professional preparation, educational resources, credible assessment, inclusion, and collective advancement supplied further purposes within this landscape. These purposes acquired specific meanings through the evaluations and practices attached to them. Assistance could release teachers’ time for educational relationships, while dependence raised concerns about understanding and professional judgment. Credible assessment could be pursued through technical safeguards or through dialogue and evidence of learning. The answer to the first research question therefore lies in these connections: the coverage described different ways of learning, teaching, and exercising judgment, with benefits and risks evaluated in relation to particular educational outcomes.

The comparison across the six SIPC dimensions showed differences in emphasis within overlapping concerns. Public/central outlets more frequently addressed collective purposes and inclusion, referred to AI without specifying its technical form, situated futures in Vietnam, and described implementation and long-term change. They also more often foregrounded public authorities, institutional leadership, and organisational responsibilities. Commercial/general outlets more frequently addressed generative AI and foreign settings, included negative evaluations and learner and expert voices, and assigned responsibility to learners. The negative-evaluation difference was smaller when only primary statements were counted, distinguishing the inclusion of criticism from its prominence. Full-denominator certainty differences require caution because coding was more often missing in public/central coverage; observed-field percentages provide a complementary comparison. These patterns answer the second research question by locating variation across purposes, evaluations, technologies, horizons, speakers, and implications rather than assigning one vision to each outlet group. The study contributes to comparative education by showing how news within a shared national setting gives visibility to different educational expectations and distributes the authority to describe change and the responsibility to realise it.
